strengths: The authors shows a study of the RSME regarding surface air temperature and precipitation for single emulator among . PACE outperfoms the other emulators on 13 models on 15 for temperature and 9 models over 15 for precipitation. A box plot summarize the overall performances regarding these 15 models. PACE is interesting for surface air temperature. It also use less parameters and is focused on advection-diffusion.
Ablations studies are performed with four climate model to justify the use of advection, diffusion and Neural ODE.
The authors made some claim on Green computing. This is a good step for the environment.
The paper is overall well-written and easy to follow.
Predicting uncertainty estimates is especially important for climate models, and previous SOTA methods are currently not performing UQ.
The proposed PACE model is significantly lightweight compared to SOTA baselines.
Efficient, accurate climate emulation is an important topic with the potential for significant impact in democratizing cheap climate projections under various greenhouse gas emission scenarios.
Using a physics-informed featurization technique based on an advection-diffusion equation is an original idea.
PACE generally is amongst the best, if not the best, performing models compared to the reported baselines, in terms of RMSE.
The authors use a standard dataset and compare against appropriate baselines.
They include an ablation study which explores the contribution of their skill to different aspects of their model.
The model appears to achieve good skill in comparison to these baselines, although I have serious misgivings about the approach and its motivation (outlined below).

Using machine learning to learn climate emulators is a highly interesting problem with potential for large impact. The authors have accurately identified that there are many open questions in the area, and in particular the ability of the machine learning models to incorporate more complex forcing from greenhouse gas emissions is a key property that needs further development.
The use of the hybrid approach with the advection-diffusion equations seems well-motivated and leads to an impressively stable model. The authors show stable rollouts for 86 years.
Compared to baseline models PACE achieves lower RMSEs for single-model evaluation. Also when training PACE as a super-emulator the errors achieved are generally lower than baselines.
A valuable ablation study is performed in section 6. This study clearly shows that all parts of the model are important for the performance of the model.
Incorporation of physical priors for climate modeling
Improvements in downstream performance over various tasks
The paper boasts outstanding results.
The idea of adding diffusion, noise and greenhouse forcings to advection ODEs is excellent.
weaknesses: Many incorrect statements lead to confusion in the manuscript. They should be corrected carefully.

In the abstract, the author claim that numerical simulations are computationally intensive and inefficient. The second term is imprecise, the authors claims in the conclusion that their model does not capture extreme events at regional level, the training having coarse resolution. Which means numerical simulations are still essential.

In the part 2.2, the authors are talking about the work of Chen et al 2018 which should be adapted for spherical mesh. This paragraph is unclear about if the improvements are valid for spherical use, and that the authors wants to adapt to their context.
The equation 1 is unclear, v and D depend on time and space.
In the equation 3, v and D depend on x,y and t. This should be clarified.

Uncertainty quantification is claimed in the title of the paper. In the results, it is showed on the figure 3 with box plot for a whole simulation and 15 models, and in the figure 4 to show the error of approximation. The uncertainty is not quantified in the remaining figures, especially in figure 1 and 8 where Gaussian noise is used.
The Gaussian noise hypothesis should be more justified. Does this comes from a Central Limit Theorem? What is uncertainties are the authors talking about?
Line 217, 219 and 254 three \sigma are used, I assume these are three different quantities and function.
In figure 4, the discretisation difference and the error are important. The authors claim that they want to improve this later.
In section 3.2.1, the scheme for the concentration C should be clarified. This is very difficult to understand.

As stated in the section 3, Earth is presented as a rectangle in section 3. and then Spherical Fourier Neural Operator and L(i) are introduced in section 4.. This is crucial and should be improved so the reader understand that the spherical geometry is well considered even with the use of section 3.
The figure 2 needs to be improved. I would use more math symbols to be consistent with the manuscript.
References regarding the models which PACE is compared against would help to understand briefly what they are.
Regarding the results of the super emulator, no reference is done to the table 2. The reader has to look for the table.

The training of PACE use simulated data, and not real observations. Authors want to extend their study to higher resolution and using physical constraint (energy, mass and water conservation in the loss function).
The authors claims regarding Green computed are too general. Quantifying and comparing the carbon footprint and energy consumption will be appreciated.
The motivation and description of CBAM is unclear.
The PACE model is only limited to surface air temperature and precipitation. Other climate models like ClimaX can predict a wide variety of target variables such as wind velocities, pressure, etc.
The paper does not compare against other recent SOTA climate models like FourCast [1] and GraphCast [2].
Grammatical errors and careless statements plague the manuscript. It should be carefully proofread.

Including ACE and LUCIE in Table 1 is unfair since they were designed for the "autoregressive" climate-dynamics emulation problem rather than the diagnostics-type emulation problem studied in this paper. The inputs-outputs are quite different between these emulation approaches. The relationship between them is more complex in the autoregressive case.
Section 3.3.: The name of the Convolution Block Attention Module (CBAM) is misleading since it contains no attention layers. Similarly for the "channel attention map" and the "spatial attention map".

The abstract mentions that "While deep learning methodologies have made significant progress in weather forecasting, they are still unstable for climate emulation tasks". This statement is wrong and misleading; it mischaracterizes the stability of existing deep learning climate emulators.

Adaptation of SFNO architecture (especially Appendix A.2) is not consistent with the configuration from LUCIE nor from ACE nor the original SFNO paper, and the paper adds a 2D convolutional layer for 4→2 channels rather than adjusting the original SFNO architecture.

I have doubts about the interpretation shown in Fig. 1. The climate models show clear increasing temperature trends, which are not properly emulated by PACE. In one case there's no clear increasing trend (is PACE simply learning the mean?), in the other case it's much smaller than the climate model one. The SSP should be indicated in the caption.
Fig. 4 shows that PACE's predictions are very pixelated, which is problematic because high spatial resolution is desirable in climate modeling.
No error bars are included; re-training with different random seeds and reporting error bars on RMSEs is recommended to assess significance of results.
Simple, non-neural approaches such as Gaussian Processes and linear regression, which perform well for diagnostic-type climate emulation, are not included for comparison.
The title and model mention uncertainty aware climate emulation, but none of the experiments study uncertainty (e.g., ensembling or comparison to CMIP6 ensembles).
Insights into training and inference runtimes of PACE and comparison to fully neural approaches that don't require ODE solvers are missing.
Can you elaborate on Eq. 14? The relationship to Eq. 13 and the rest of the paper is not clear; it is unclear what $y$, $\,sigma^2$ represent and how they are chosen.
Information about the periodic boundary condition (PBC) is completely missing; the manuscript only states that PBC is used to simulate the entire planet without further discussion.
It is not clear how/where the "harmonic embeddings" are used in PACE; the diagram does not show them and their definition suggests they are temporal rather than spatio‑temporal.
Fig. 2 diagram indicates an "Adaptive Pooling" module at the end of PACE, but no information about this module is provided elsewhere in the manuscript.

The spatial attention map outputs are squished to (0, 1) by a sigmoid, which does not seem to match the range of the standardized targets, raising concerns about the need for the adaptive pooling module.

How exactly is a Neural ODE used inside PACE? The paper says it uses the dopri5 ODE solver, which is a traditional method not based on neural networks, contradicting the claim that a Neural ODE is used.

The authors use a 2‑D advection diffusion model as the basis for their NeuralODE, which is not a sensible approximation for climate dynamics; the atmosphere follows Navier‑Stokes and emissions have no diffusion, undermining the rationale for the NeuralODE and coefficient estimates in 3.2.1.

The claim that the paper frames climate emulation in a new setting due to inadequacies in autoregressive models is false; the baseline dataset ClimateSet already uses this framing, and prior work has established this approach.
The discussion of periodic boundary conditions (3.2.3) is confusing, conflating spatial periodicity of the Earth with temporal periodicity modeled by harmonic embeddings.

Evaluating models against the full 2015‑2100 period of SSP245 and comparing against the first 10 years (Figure 8) is misguided; the standard protocol evaluates against the last 20 years because early years are too similar to training scenarios.

The presentation of the model throughout section 3 is incoherent and hard to understand, making it difficult to see how different parts fit together. Specifically: what is the shape of $F$ in section 3.3 and how does it relate to each $u$ in section 3.1?; after time 0, where do $v_x$ and $v_y$ in eq. 6 come from?; the deep‑learning components in section 3.3 are described as "attention map/module" but do not implement any attention mechanism.

Periodic boundary conditions as described treat the Earth as a torus rather than a sphere; applying them in latitude forces the values at the south pole to equal those at the north pole, which is undesirable.
The uncertainty estimation part of the model (section 3.2.2) is unclear: the covariance structure of the Gaussian process $\eta$ added to the advection‑diffusion equation is not specified.

It is unclear where the $\mu$ and $\sigma$ used in the NLL loss originate; the notation suggests $\sigma$ is the same as for the Gaussian process, which is atypical for prediction uncertainty, and the Gaussian assumption may be overly simplistic.
The model's capability to capture uncertainty is never evaluated; only RMSE is reported, which nullifies the claimed uncertainty‑aware contribution.

Using RMSE with respect to the actual atmospheric state (temperature and precipitation) may be less relevant for climate emulation, where capturing overall statistics and trends is more important than day‑by‑day accuracy.
Results for the full model are missing for comparison in Figure 5.
The abstract incorrectly states that PACE is trained only on greenhouse gas emissions data, while it also uses temperature and precipitation data for training.
Claims in the fourth paragraph of section 1 should be supported by references.
Several highly related works (e.g., Salva Rühling et al., 2024; Kochkov et al., 2024) are missing from the related‑work discussion.

Descriptions of baseline models and the multi‑head decoder rely entirely on referencing ClimateSet, making the paper feel not self‑contained and experiments hard to follow without consulting the ClimateSet paper.
The paper is not well written.
The paper misses a large number of related works that also utilize physics priors for climate and weather modeling (e.g., ClimODE, Neural GCM, WeatherGFT) and provides no comparisons to them.
Since the forecasts are probabilistic, it would be better to use CRPS scores rather than RMSE for evaluation.

The language of the paper is weak, hurting clarity and message; many sentences are oddly phrased, notation is imprecise, there are hanging equations, poor formatting, and figures are poorly formatted, making experiments and results difficult to follow.

It is unclear what the paper actually does; the model appears to learn to match outputs of an existing climate simulator, but the operation of the ODE and role of the neural networks are not explained, and the source of GHG emissions for future years is unspecified.

The method contributions of the noise process, diffusion constant estimation, and boundary conditions are unconvincing; the noise process is not presented as a proper Wiener process, the diffusion constant estimation lacks motivation, and boundary conditions are not convincingly implemented.
